item.title: "Illuminating" the silkworm chassis: Synthetic biology-driven evolution of genetic-based sexing circuits.
item.abstract: The silkworm (Bombyx mori), a classical lepidopteran model, is evolving into a highly tractable synthetic biology chassis. In modern sericulture, genetic sexing circuits provide a rational design framework for efficient all-male rearing, effectively overcoming the gene dosage disruptions and fitness costs associated with traditional radiation-induced chromosomal translocations. This review systematically summarizes the construction strategies and industrial applications of these circuits. We outline the optimization of sex determination elements and highlight the advantages of far-red optical markers in penetrating host physical barriers and reducing cytotoxicity. Furthermore, we trace the evolution of genomic manipulation tools from random transposon insertions to targeted CRISPR/Cas9 integration into genomic safe harbors (GSHs). To address circuit instability during multigenerational rearing, protective molecular strategies-including boundary insulators, conditional expression, and automatic excision networks-are evaluated. We also explore the industrial interface that integrates standardized biological optical reporters with artificial intelligence and high-throughput optoelectronic sorting hardware. Ultimately, engineering principles derived from the silkworm chassis can provide a molecular framework for the sterile insect technique in global pest management, with future directions pointing toward footprint-free genome editing and dynamic conditional regulation.

item.title: Adaptation of a Fluorogenic RNA to N1-Methylpseudouridine Nucleoside Chemistry.
item.abstract: N1-methylpseudouridine (mΨ) is a modified nucleoside that entirely replaces uridine in the design of many therapeutic messenger RNAs (mRNA) to alleviate their intrinsic immunogenicity while preserving their capacity to be translated into protein. However, the impact of such replacement in functional non-coding RNAs has only been scarcely studied, and most studies have shown impairment in the function of the tested RNAs thereby limiting their potential applications. In this work, we further show that exchanging uridines by mΨ in green-emitting Fluorogenic Light-up Aptamers (FLAP) is detrimental to their capacity of binding and enhancing the fluorescence of their cognate fluorogen. Moreover, combining directed evolution and rational design allowed not only to pinpoint the structural elements impacted by the replacement of uridine by mΨ, but also to re-establish the function of a mΨ-modified non-coding RNA for the first time. This yielded Ψ-Spinach, a FLAP suited for the precise labelling of mΨ-modified mRNA and usable for human cells transfection. This work thus paves the way for the adaptation of other functional non-coding RNAs with mΨ in view of engineering and optimizing therapeutic modified mRNAs.

item.title: Directed Evolution of the Cbx1 Chromodomain Generates a High-Affinity Trimethyllysine-Binding Variant.
item.abstract: Directed evolution is a powerful and versatile strategy for engineering proteins with enhanced affinity and tailored molecular recognition properties. Here, we applied phage display-guided directed evolution to enhance the binding of the wild-type Cbx1 chromodomain (Cbx1-CD) to an H3K9me3-containing peptide. Screening a soft-randomized library targeting residues surrounding the aromatic cage yielded C29, which bound the H3K9me3 peptide with a KD of 57 nM and exhibited an approximately 14-fold lower dissociation rate constant than Cbx1-CD. Across an H3K9me3-derived alanine-scanning series and a peptide panel, C29 showed stronger binding signals than Cbx1-CD for multiple peptides containing trimethyllysine (Kme3), suggesting lower flanking-sequence dependence for C29 than for Cbx1-CD. An AlphaFold3 model of the C29-H3K9me3 complex suggested local changes in the hydrophobic and electrostatic environment surrounding the Kme3-binding pocket, providing a mechanistic hypothesis for C29's enhanced affinity and reduced flanking-sequence dependence. When two Kme3-containing peptides were spiked into a 100-fold molar excess of unmodified background peptides, C29-conjugated beads effectively enriched both Kme3 peptides relative to the unmodified background. These findings define C29 as a high-affinity Kme3-binding Cbx1 chromodomain variant and support its further evaluation as an affinity reagent for Kme3-containing peptide enrichment.

item.title: Rational Engineering of Carboxylic Acid Reductase for Improved Catalytic Efficiency and Substrate Tolerance Enabling Green Vanillin Biosynthesis.
item.abstract: Vanillin is a high-value natural aromatic compound widely used in food, flavor, and pharmaceutical fields. Carboxylic acid reductase (CAR)-catalyzed vanillic acid bioreduction offers a green vanillin biosynthesis route, yet low catalytic activity and severe substrate inhibition limit its industrial application. Herein, we screened 10 bacterial CAR homologues and constructed superior chimeric CAR templates via domain recombination. Combined with structure-guided directed evolution and substrate tunnel remodeling, the optimized quadruple mutant M4 was obtained, exhibiting 4-fold higher catalytic efficiency compared with the wild-type MavCAR (and 1.6-fold higher than the parental chimera M0) and partially relieved activity decline at elevated substrate concentrations. Structural simulations clarified that tunnel expansion and hydrogen bond remodeling synergistically stabilized enzyme-substrate binding. The M4-based whole-cell system achieved 95% vanillin conversion (8.7 g·L-1) from 10 g·L-1 vanillic acid, and a two-step cascade system realized efficient de novo vanillin synthesis from glucose. This work provides a robust engineered CAR biocatalyst for green vanillin preparative-scale biosynthesis.

item.title: Atroposelective Construction of Tetra-ortho-Substituted Dibenz[c,e]azepines Using an Engineered Imine Reductase.
item.abstract: Atropisomeric dibenz[c,e]azepines are privileged scaffolds in asymmetric synthesis, medicinal chemistry, and materials science, yet their atroposelective preparation remains challenging due to the difficulty of controlling axial chirality while constructing a strained medium-sized ring. Tetra-ortho-substituted dibenz[c,e]azepines are especially elusive, with no catalytic asymmetric method reported owing to extreme steric hindrance. Here, we report the first biocatalytic strategy for the atroposelective synthesis of these congested bridged biaryls, employing an engineered imine reductase (IRED) that catalyzes a sequential inter- and intramolecular reductive amination cascade. Structure-guided directed evolution of an IRED from Streptomyces tricolor provided a triple mutant (IRED-04-M3) that delivers various tetra-ortho-substituted dibenz[c,e]azepines in high yields with excellent atroposelectivity (up to 97% yield, >99:1 er) by dynamic kinetic resolution. Gram-scale preparation was also demonstrated. Mechanistic studies and molecular dynamics simulations provide insight into the cascade reaction and stereocontrol exerted by the engineered enzyme.

item.title: Binding pocket optimization of Pueraria mirifica type II chalcone isomerase synergizing with a necrosis-attenuating host transcription factor for persistent daidzein biosynthesis.
item.abstract: Pathway reconstitution of leguminous isoflavonoids in non-legume plant chassis offers a tractably controlled environment to probe specialized metabolism, yet it remains critically bottlenecked by suboptimal heterologous enzyme efficiency and severe host tissue necrosis. Here, we overcome these long-standing architectural limitations by establishing a highly synergistic, necrosis-attenuated Nicotiana benthamiana synthetic biology platform. We characterized chalcone isomerases from Pueraria mirifica (PmCHIs), revealing that PmCHI Type II operates as a biochemical junction exhibiting a specialized substrate-dependent alkaline optimum (pH 7.5-8.0) exclusively toward isoliquiritigenin. Combining 500-ns molecular dynamics simulations with structure-guided mutagenesis, active-site engineering identified an I195V variant with enhanced isoliquiritigenin preference. The conservative I195V substitution was predicted to reduce local steric crowding and produced an isoliquiritigenin selectivity ratio of 1.63 in vitro. For in planta pathway integration, we delivered a polycistronic cascade using P2A ribosome-skipping peptides to streamline multiplex multi-gene stacking. Crucially, substituting the conventional Arabidopsis thaliana MYB12 regulator with a host-derived N. benthamiana MYB60 transcription factor successfully attenuated tissue necrosis, accompanied by reduced electrolyte leakage. Quantitative proteomics showed no statistically significant difference in PmCHI abundance between the I195V and WT-II treatments in planta, while independent plant batches consistently showed higher daidzein accumulation with I195V, although the magnitude of enhancement varied among experiments. The NbMYB60-based platform extended the operational viability window up to 9 days, delivering a robust daidzein titer of 1.5 mg/g DW at 6 days post-infiltration, with individual high-performing replicates reaching up to 2.5 mg/g DW. Together, these results establish an integrated enzyme-engineering and necrosis-attenuating regulatory framework for persistent daidzein biosynthesis and specialized pathway reconstitution in planta.

item.title: Conditional genetic manipulation systems in mosquitoes: Progress, Challenges, and perspectives.
item.abstract: Mosquitoes are major vectors of severe infectious diseases, including malaria, dengue fever, and chikungunya, and continue to pose a substantial threat to global public health. A comprehensive understanding of mosquito-pathogen interactions, disease transmission mechanisms, and ecological adaptations is essential for developing innovative strategies to control mosquito-borne diseases. In recent years, genetic manipulation technologies have greatly advanced functional genomics research in mosquitoes; however, their limited spatiotemporal precision restricts the functional characterization of essential genes, key developmental regulators, and tissue-specific genes, often due to embryonic or early developmental lethality, systemic editing effects, and complex phenotypic consequences. As an important strategy for precision genetic regulation, Conditional Genetic Manipulation Systems (CGMSs) utilize tissue-specific, developmental stage-specific, or externally inducible regulatory elements to achieve controlled expression of functional genetic components (e.g., Cas9), thereby enabling spatiotemporally precise genetic modifications. These systems provide a new research paradigm for investigating mosquito basic biology and developing genetic control technologies. This review systematically summarizes the major types, regulatory mechanisms, and current advances of CGMSs in mosquitoes, with particular emphasis on different regulatory elements and their applications in functional gene analysis, studies of pathogen transmission mechanisms, and vector control strategies. Furthermore, we discuss future directions for expanding editing systems and developing genetic manipulation resources, aiming to provide insights into the construction of precise genetic manipulation systems in mosquitoes and other insects and the advancement of next-generation genetic control technologies.

item.title: Unleashing the industrial potential of microbial plant cell wall polysaccharide-degrading enzymes: recent advances in protein engineering.
item.abstract: Plant cell wall polysaccharide-degrading enzymes (PCWPEs) used in industry are predominantly of microbial origin. Key enzyme classes, including cellulases, lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs), β-xylanases, β-mannanases and pectinases, have attained technological maturity and are widely deployed across agro-waste biorefineries, food and feed processing, textile and pulp manufacturing. Low catalytic efficiency, insufficient thermostability, poor operational adaptability, restricted functionality, and product inhibition limit the industrial use of these enzymes. Structure- and sequence-guided design, supported by computational design tools, now allows more targeted improvement of PCWPE performance. Yet, the stringent and context-specific performance requirements imposed by diverse industrial applications continue to present substantial challenges. This review systematically summarizes current engineering strategies for PCWPEs in the past decade, aiming to provide a comprehensive understanding of the tailored strategies employed in different engineering directions and to offer insightful proposals for future research.

item.title: Multimodal functional characterization of the LDLR noncoding landscape
item.abstract: The expression level of the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) gene is a critical determinant of circulating low-density lipoprotein concentrations and the corresponding risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. While the importance of sterol response elements in LDLR transcriptional regulation has been firmly established, the functional contribution of other potential cis-regulatory elements (CREs) remains poorly understood. In this study, we developed and applied a variety of high throughput functional genomic tools to systematically interrogate the noncoding space at the LDLR locus. These included saturation CRISPR nuclease, CRISPR activation, and CRISPR inhibition screening as well as a massively parallel reporter assay. With each approach, we observed robust discrimination of control sequences and significant effects for other regions with a previously unrecognized influence on LDLR expression. The CREs identified by each modality were overlapping but distinct, both in relation to each other and to those regions predicted to harbor CRE activity. Collectively, our findings clarify the functional landscape of the LDLR locus and highlight the complementary nature of different functional genomic approaches to CRE identification.

item.title: Conserved Brain-Associated CD8+ T Cell Programs and Their Regulation by the Brain Microenvironment
item.abstract: CD8+ T cells are increasingly recognized as components of the healthy brain, yet whether their specialized functional characteristics are conserved across species and how the brain microenvironment regulates their effector programs remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized brain-associated CD8+ T cells in the common marmoset and investigated their regulation by brain-derived signals. Flow cytometric analysis revealed a substantial population of CD8+ T cells in the healthy marmoset brain parenchyma that exhibited high IFN-{gamma} competence but minimal granzyme B (GzmB) expression, resembling the functional phenotype previously identified in mice. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of mouse and marmoset CD8+ T cells revealed tissue-associated transcriptional heterogeneity and distinct differentiation- and effector-associated programs. To investigate how the brain microenvironment shapes these characteristics, we exposed activated mouse CD8+ T cells to brain lysate and performed targeted CRISPR interference screening of 107 cell-surface receptor genes coupled with single-cell RNA sequencing. Brain lysate selectively reduced Gzmb and Ifng expression while increasing Tnf and Xcl1, indicating differential regulation of cytotoxic and inflammatory effector programs. Receptor perturbations revealed heterogeneous transcriptional responses and identified candidate pathways potentially involved in sensing brain-derived signals. Together, these findings identify shared functional characteristics of brain-associated CD8+ T cells across rodents and nonhuman primates and establish a framework for understanding how the neural microenvironment shapes adaptive immune function.
item.authors: Park, K.,  Sanchez, T.,  Jeon, S.,  Schade, P. F.,  Hildebrand, D. G. C.,  Yim,

item.title: Noninvasive Detection and Subtyping of Esophageal Cancer by Circulating Cell-Free mtDNA Fragmentomics: A Multi-Center Validation Study.
item.abstract: Esophageal cancer (EC) is highly lethal due to late diagnosis, and accurate non-invasive tools for early detection and subtyping remain lacking. Circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) fragmentomics offers a promising biomarker source. In this large multi-center study enrolling 1,260 participants spanning healthy control (HC), benign esophageal diseases (BED), precancerous lesions and EC patients, we developed two machine learning models based on plasma ccf-mtDNA fragmentomic profiles: an EC detection (ED) model and a pathological subtyping prediction (PSP) model. The ED model achieved an AUC of 0.9706 (EC vs. non-EC) in the training cohort, with high performance in internal (0.9762), external (0.9748), and Chinese minority (0.9668, Uyghur and Kazakh) validation cohorts. At the optimal cut-off, it yielded 92.16% sensitivity for stage I EC in the combined validation cohort and correctly identified 93.10% of early EC cases missed by preoperative biopsy. It also discriminated high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia from non-EC with an AUC of 0.9597. The PSP model distinguished ESCC from EAC with 89.71% accuracy, improving to 90.74% after integrating key clinical parameters. In summary, ccf-mtDNA fragmentomics provides a robust, non-invasive platform for early EC detection, precancerous risk stratification, and histological subtyping, demonstrating strong potential to transform clinical management.

item.title: Toward a digital urinary biopsy for early risk stratification in diabetic kidney disease: Anchoring shed cells, vesicles, and cell-free DNA to spatial kidney cell states.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease worldwide. However, albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which define and stage DKD, report established injury and do not resolve the cellular heterogeneity underlying variable progression. Urine, the only biofluid to traverse every nephron segment, carries shed cells, extracellular vesicles (EVs) and cell-free DNA (cfDNA), each retaining information about its cell of origin.
MAIN BODY: This review develops the concept of a digital urinary biopsy, in which the three compartments are read together against spatial single-cell kidney atlases to infer non-invasively which cell states are active and whether niche-associated programs are engaged, an approach we term atlas-anchored molecular profiling. For each compartment, we tabulate study population, sample size, processing, assay, performance and validation status. Because shed-cell RNA, selectively sorted vesicle cargo and cfDNA methylation differ in origin, measurement scale and bias, each requires its own reference matrix, sampling function and background terms. All three carry renal information in feasibility studies, yet none is a validated clinical assay in DKD. Moreover, a cfDNA methylation reference at the required resolution is lacking, and no named computational method has been tested on urine.
CONCLUSION: We therefore present the framework as a structured research hypothesis and define the required validation, from analytical and clinical validity to prospective demonstration of utility, with non-albuminuric DKD, which albuminuria-based screening misses, as the index use case. It offers a testable route to cell-resolved, non-invasive staging of DKD rather than a demonstrated capability.

item.title: Assessment of a direct fluorescence-based cell-free DNA assay for evaluating the extent of metastatic dissemination: An exploratory study.
item.abstract: Fluorescence-based cell-free DNA (cfDNA) assays quantify nucleic acids without the need for DNA extraction and amplification. The present study investigated whether cfDNA levels differed between patients with active cancer and those with no evidence of disease (NED). Blood samples from patients with metastatic cancer (Patient group) and from individuals with NED (patients that had completed curative-intent treatment and remained recurrence free for ≥1 year; NED group) were used to quantify cfDNA levels using PicoGreen™ reagent. In total, 124 participants were prospectively enrolled between January 2020 and August 2021 (Patient group, n=72; NED group, n=52). The median age was 69 years (range: 27-83 years) in the Patient group and 65 years (range: 34-81 years) in the NED group. In the Patient group, the pancreatobiliary (n=32, 44.4%), genitourinary (n=20, 27.7%) and gastrointestinal (n=6, 8.3%) sites were the most common primary cancer sites. The median cfDNA value in the Patient group (9.80 µg/ml, IQR 8.63-11.08) was significantly higher than that in the NED group (8.40 µg/ml, IQR 7.75-9.10, P<0.001). In addition, the median cfDNA levels were significantly higher in patients with a high extent of metastatic dissemination (defined as metastases in three or more organs) than in those with a low tumor extent (10.70 µg/ml, IQR 9.35-12.4 vs. 9.45 µg/ml, IQR 8.48-10.85, respectively; P=0.027). Notably, there was no significant correlation between cfDNA and conventional tumor marker levels, including carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels (P=0.468 and P=0.134, respectively). These findings indicated that cfDNA levels were elevated in patients with metastatic cancer compared with those with NED, particularly in those with a higher extent of metastatic dissemination. Additionally, cfDNA levels were not correlated with those of conventional tumor markers. These cross-sectional exploratory data highlight the potential utility of fluorescence-based cfDNA assays in assessing the extent of metastatic dissemination, and provide a foundational rationale for future longitudinal studies investigating treatment monitoring and prognosis.

item.title: Clinical Utility of Plasma Microbial Cell-Free DNA Sequencing in Adult Immunocompromised Patients: A Real-World Cohort Study.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Plasma metagenomic next generation sequencing (mNGS) enables noninvasive pathogen detection independent of organism viability. Although analytic performance has been described, the real-world clinical impact in immunocompromised hosts remains incompletely defined.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of immunocompromised adults undergoing plasma mNGS testing from January 2022 through November 2024 at the Medical University of South Carolina. Immunocompromised conditions included solid organ transplantation, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, active hematologic malignancy, HIV, or biologic immunosuppressants. Clinical impact was adjudicated by infectious disease physicians as positive, negative, or neutral. Positive results were classified as definite, probable, possible, or unlikely infectious based on clinical correlation and concordance with conventional microbiologic testing (CMT).
RESULTS: Ninety-eight patients were included (median age 60 years [range 18-76]; 63% male), including solid organ transplant (31%), hematopoietic stem cell transplant (8%), HIV (13%), active malignancy (42%), corticosteroids (3%), and biologic therapy (10%). At testing, 85% were receiving antimicrobials and 88% were hospitalized. Plasma mNGS was positive in 62% of cases, with CMT concordance in 30%. Thirty-two percent of tests had positive clinical impact, identifying unrecognized infection or antimicrobial optimization. Sixty-six percent had no treatment impact and 2% had potential negative impact. More than half of discordant positives were deemed possible or unlikely infections. False-negative cases included invasive mold and nontuberculous mycobacterial infections.
CONCLUSIONS: In this antimicrobial-exposed immunocompromised cohort, plasma mNGS frequently detected organisms but less often influenced clinical management. Discordant positives were common, and false negatives occurred in selected syndromes, supporting cautious interpretation and stewardship-guided use.

item.title: Ginsenoside Re attenuates severe acute pancreatitis-associated acute lung injury by inhibiting pancreatic necroptosis-driven cfDNA release and pulmonary cGAS-STING activation.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The high mortality of severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) is primarily driven by multiple organ dysfunction, particularly acute lung injury (ALI), a condition for which lacks specific pharmacological therapy. Ginsenoside Re (Re) has documented anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, with preliminary evidence indicating its protective potential in pancreatic injury. However, its precise therapeutic efficacy and underlying mechanisms in SAP, especially concerning the mitigation of systemic complications, remain incompletely understood.
PURPOSE: This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of Re in SAP and to delineate the underlying mechanistic pathway connecting pancreatic acinar cell death to pulmonary injury.
METHODS: SAP was induced in mice by seven hourly cerulein injections followed by a final lipopolysaccharide challenge, and Re was administered intraperitoneally during the induction period. Primary pancreatic acinar cells (PACs) were isolated, and mouse pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells (PMVECs) were cultured for in vitro studies. Underlying mechanisms were investigated through transcriptomic and network pharmacology analyses, followed by molecular docking and experimental validation.
RESULTS: Re treatment significantly alleviated pancreatic injury in SAP mice, with a pronounced reduction in acinar necrosis. Integrated transcriptomic and network pharmacology analyses identified necroptosis as a key target for these effects. Accordingly, Re inhibited RIPK3/MLKL-mediated necroptosis both in vivo and in vitro. The specific RIPK3 inhibitor GSK872 abolished cfDNA release from PACs, indicating that necroptosis is the primary source of cfDNA, and notably, Re mimicked these effects. Acinar cell-derived cfDNA was shown to induce pulmonary endothelial inflammation and barrier dysfunction via activation of the cGAS-STING pathway, effects that were abolished by DNase I. In addition, correlation analysis showed that mouse serum cfDNA levels were positively correlated with lung injury parameters. Further pulmonary transcriptomic analysis confirmed that Re treatment suppressed cfDNA-triggered activation of the cGAS-STING signaling in vivo, thereby contributing to the significant attenuation of lung injury.
CONCLUSION: Our study uncovers a novel pathological axis in SAP-ALI, wherein pancreatic necroptosis drives cfDNA release, which subsequently activates the pulmonary endothelial cGAS-STING signaling, ultimately leading to distant lung injury. Re interrupts this cascade at multiple nodes, primarily by inhibiting acinar necroptosis and thereby limiting cfDNA release, which in turn attenuates both local and systemic organ injuries. Together, these findings elucidate a novel mechanistic basis for SAP-ALI and support Re as a promising multi-target therapeutic agent for SAP.
